title: Behavior-chain detection for T1133 External Remote Services across Windows, Linux, macOS, Containers
shortTitle: Behavior-chain detection for T1133 External Remote Servic...
summary: This strategy covers T1133 External Remote Services, the abuse of legitimate remote access services such as virtual private network (VPN) gateways, remote desktop gateways and third-party support tools to enter an environment. Attackers rarely need to exploit anything: they sign in with valid credentials obtained earlier, often with no multi-factor prompt, and blend into the same logs that record normal remote work. The detection is therefore behaviour-chain based, correlating authentication events from the gateway with what the session does next on the host, including new service creation, unusual internal scanning and access to file shares. It requires identity provider or VPN logs joined to host logon and process telemetry. It fails most often because gateway logs live with the network team while host logs live with the security team, so the two halves of the chain are never joined.

beginner.definition: This detection watches the remote access services that let people work from outside the office. These include virtual private networks, which are private tunnels over the internet, and remote desktop gateways. The detection looks for logins that seem wrong, not for broken software.
beginner.whyItMatters: Remote access is a front door that must stay open for staff. An intruder who steals one password can walk through it. The login looks normal in the records. Only the activity after the login shows that the person is not the real owner of the account.
howItWorks: The gateway records each remote login, including the account name, the source address and the result.
The security log on the target host records which account was used and how long the session lasted.
Process records show what the session started, such as new services or administrative tools.
The rule joins these sources by account name and host within a short time window.
A login from an unusual country or at an odd hour, followed by administrative commands, raises an alert.
beginner.example: Think of a hospital sign-in sheet at a staff entrance. The sheet shows a real badge number and a correct time, so the guard waves the person through. The problem only appears later, when the same badge opens the drug store and the records office in ten minutes.
takeaways: Valid credentials used from outside are the main risk, not software bugs.
A remote login only becomes suspicious when you look at what happened next.
Joining gateway records with host records is what turns two weak signals into one strong one.

objectives: Describe how external remote services are abused with valid accounts instead of exploits
List the gateway and host telemetry needed to rebuild a remote session
Correlate a remote authentication event with the first administrative actions on the host
Identify baseline login patterns such as normal hours and expected source regions
Decide which remote access services are in scope for monitoring and which are not
Explain why impossible travel and geo-velocity signals alone produce weak alerts
dataSources: VPN or remote access gateway authentication logs with account name, source IP address, result and session duration
Windows Security event 4624 logon type 3 and logon type 10 with source workstation name and IP address
Linux sshd authentication records showing accepted publickey or password logins with source address
Windows Security event 7045 or System log service installation records on the session host
Process creation telemetry from Sysmon event 1 or Windows Security event 4688 covering the first minutes of the session
logic: The pattern is a remote authentication that succeeds from an untrusted source and is followed within a short window by host actions that the account does not normally perform. Analysts correlate the gateway or security log authentication (account, source address, timestamp, logon type) with the host telemetry that follows: new service installation, creation of local accounts, or execution of administrative utilities. The benign case is an employee who connects from a known region at a normal hour and then opens mail and files; the malicious case is the same login from an unexpected network, at an odd time, followed by discovery or persistence commands on a server the account has never touched. Distinguishing them needs a per-account baseline, not a fixed rule.
pseudoQuery:
# title: Remote access login followed by suspicious host activity
# logsource:
#   product: windows
#   service: security
# detection:
#   selection_logon:
#     EventID: 4624
#     LogonType:
#       - 3
#       - 10
#   filter_trusted:
#     IpAddress|startswith:
#       - '10.'
#       - '192.168.'
#   selection_follow:
#     EventID: 7045
#   condition: selection_logon and not filter_trusted and selection_follow
# level: medium
falsePositives: Engineers on call who connect from a home network or hotel outside the usual corporate address ranges
Third-party support vendors who use a shared remote access account and then run approved maintenance scripts
Business travellers whose sign-in times follow local time zones rather than headquarters time
Automated backup or monitoring jobs that authenticate to remote services from a jump host on a schedule
tuningNotes: Baseline the source address ranges, accounts and hours for each remote access service over at least thirty days, then express the baseline as filter lists rather than as a single country block, since cloud egress addresses change often. Add the account to the alert only when it has not been used from that source range before, and suppress service accounts that hold scheduled maintenance windows. Restrict the rule to servers and to accounts with administrative rights to cut volume sharply. The trade-off is that a compromised ordinary user account that only reads mail and files will no longer alert, so keep a lighter rule for those accounts that watches for data staging or new device enrolment.
